planting.note: Direct sow an inch deep after soil has warmed following last frost, since this vigorous vining type sets fruit best once nights stay reliably above 55°F.

directions: Improved White Spine is a refinement of the old American Early White Spine type, selected in the late 19th century for a shorter, blockier fruit than its predecessor. Vines produce dark green, white-spined cucumbers 5-7 inches long with crisp, mild, pure-white flesh that stays sweet without turning bitter in warm weather. It was once a dominant market and home-garden slicer before modern burpless and disease-resistant hybrids largely replaced it, but open-pollinated seed has been kept alive by heirloom seed savers. Grow on a trellis to keep fruit straight and off the soil, and pick regularly at 5-7 inches to keep vines productive through the season.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; this earlier, shorter-vined release in the Wisconsin SMR breeding line matures a bit faster than its better-known successor, Wisconsin SMR 58.

directions: Wisconsin SMR 18 (Smooth/Spot Mosaic Resistant) came out of the University of Wisconsin cucumber breeding program that also produced the longer-running Wisconsin SMR 58, bred to resist scab and mosaic virus in a period when those diseases devastated Midwest pickling cucumber crops. It is an open-pollinated, gynoecious-leaning vining type that sets fruit a touch earlier than SMR 58, producing straight, blocky, medium-green fruit best picked small for dills or gherkins. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate plantings from other cucumber varieties if saving seed. Keep fruit picked every day or two at peak production to prevent oversized cucumbers from signaling the vine to stop setting new ones.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past last frost, since this early-maturing 19th-century type was prized for extending the watermelon season into cooler regions.

directions: Ice Cream is a 19th-century American heirloom watermelon, also sold historically as Peerless, grown round with pale greenish-white rind. The original white-fleshed, white-seeded strain dates to around 1860; a sweeter pink-fleshed, black-seeded form was being offered by Philadelphia seedsmen by the early 1870s and became the more widely grown version. Its notably early maturity and tolerance of cooler nights made it a favorite in northern growing regions that struggled to ripen larger southern watermelon types. Sow in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil after the soil has warmed, and reduce watering as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sweetness.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed well past last frost, giving vines plenty of room to ramble.

directions: Wilson's Sweet is an American heirloom watermelon offered commercially by several seed companies by the mid-20th century before falling out of wide circulation and being kept going mainly through preservation seed banks and dedicated growers. Fruit is round to oval with a distinctive mottled, spotted green rind and crisp, deep red flesh known for unusually high sweetness. Give vines generous spacing to sprawl in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and keep watering even through fruit set, tapering off as melons approach ripeness to help sugars concentrate. Because it is open-pollinated, isolated plantings allow home gardeners to save true seed from year to year.

common_name: Vine Peach Melon (Mango Melon, Chito Melon)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; vines are smaller and less sprawling than typical cantaloupe or watermelon vines.

directions: Vine Peach, also sold as Mango Melon or Chito Melon, is a small, smooth-skinned melon that ripens to pale yellow and is roughly the size and shape of a peach. It was introduced to American gardens in the 1880s and grown chiefly for preserving rather than fresh eating, since the firm, low-sugar flesh is bland raw but takes well to pickling, spiced preserves, and mock-mango or mock-pineapple recipes. Its compact vines and relatively quick maturity make it workable in shorter-season gardens that struggle with larger melons. Harvest once fruit turns fully yellow and gives slightly at the blossom end, and handle gently since the thin skin bruises easily.
